::: {.callout-note title="Running the code in this tutorial"}
Every code chunk here is tagged with `#| eval: false`, so the published page shows the code **without running it**. To run it yourself, open the downloaded `.qmd` in **RStudio**:

- **Run one chunk:** click the green ▶ (*Run Current Chunk*) at the chunk's top-right, or press *Ctrl/Cmd + Enter*. This runs the chunk **regardless of its `eval` setting** — the easiest way to work through the tutorial interactively.
- **Run a chunk on render:** change that chunk's `#| eval: false` to `#| eval: true` (or delete the line) so it executes when the document is rendered.
- **Render the whole tutorial:** click the **Render** button in RStudio (or run `quarto render` in a terminal) to execute the chunks top-to-bottom and knit a finished HTML. To run everything on render, set `eval: true` once in the YAML header at the top.
:::


## About this tutorial

This is the **runnable companion** to the P1 reading — the first hour of the optional **Tuesday (Day 0)** computational refresher. The reading builds the mental model (how computers work, what an HPC cluster is); here you actually **do it on your laptop**: install and configure VS Code, install the Quarto and R extensions, open a project folder, edit a `.qmd` file, use the integrated terminal, and run R locally. By the end you will have a fully configured local editor — your workhorse for the laptop-based tutorials throughout the week.

**Talapas and the cluster come on Friday.** Connecting VS Code to the UO HPC cluster over Remote-SSH, navigating the file systems, and running SLURM jobs is the Friday-morning track — [Module 09 — VS Code & SLURM Basics on Talapas](Tutorial_09_SLURM_Basics.html). Today is entirely on your own machine.

::: callout-note
**Companion lecture:** [Lecture P1 — Computer Systems](../Lecture_Folder/Lecture_P1_Computer_Systems.html) · **Companion reading:** [Chapter P1 — Computer Systems](../Resources_Folder/Chapter_P1_Computer_Systems.html).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="How to use this page"}
The rendered HTML shows the commands but does **not** execute them. To work along, download the source — <a href="Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd.txt" download="Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd">Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd</a> — then **drop the trailing `.txt`** so the filename ends in `.qmd`, and open it in **VS Code** (or RStudio). The shell commands are meant to be typed into a **local terminal on your laptop**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Before you start

You need two things in place before the steps below:

1.  A laptop running **Windows**, **macOS**, or **Linux** with administrator rights (so you can install software).
2.  **R installed locally.** Download the current release from [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/) if you have not already. On macOS and Windows, the installer handles everything; on Linux, install via your package manager (e.g. `sudo apt install r-base` on Ubuntu/Debian).

Throughout this tutorial, steps are the same across operating systems unless otherwise noted. Shell commands shown in code blocks are meant to be run in a **local terminal** (Terminal on macOS/Linux, PowerShell or Git Bash on Windows).

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
Why do we spend time setting up an editor before touching any data? What does a good editor buy you compared with writing code in a plain text file?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

A modern editor like VS Code gives you **syntax highlighting** (so you can read code faster), **autocompletion** (fewer typos), an **integrated terminal** (run commands without leaving the editor), and **extension ecosystem** (language servers, linters, version control, remote-connection tools). More practically for this workshop: Quarto's `.qmd` files mix prose and code blocks, and VS Code's Quarto extension lets you preview the rendered output, run individual chunks, and navigate sections — none of which a plain text file supports. The time you invest now pays off in every subsequent tutorial.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Install and open VS Code

**Visual Studio Code** is a free, cross-platform editor from Microsoft. It lets you browse and edit files, run code in an integrated terminal, and (with extensions) preview rendered Quarto documents — all without leaving the editor.

1.  Download it from <https://code.visualstudio.com/download> and run the installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
2.  Launch VS Code. Allow any permissions it requests on first start.
3.  Take a moment to find the **Activity Bar** down the left edge — the icons there switch between the Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, and (after the next step) Remote Explorer panels.
4.  Open the **Command Palette** with **Ctrl+Shift+P** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+Shift+P** (macOS). This is how you access almost every VS Code command; you will use it constantly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Install the Quarto and R extensions

In the left **Activity Bar**, click the **Extensions** icon (the four-squares icon), then search for and install:

-   **Quarto** — edit, preview, and run `.qmd` files (the workshop tutorials).
-   **R** — R language support: syntax highlighting, autocompletion, and sending code to an R terminal.

Also useful so you can open the plots and tables your scripts produce without leaving the editor:

-   **vscode-pdf** — PDF viewer.
-   **Excel Viewer** — renders `.csv` files as a formatted table.

After installing, restart VS Code if prompted.

::: {.callout-note title="Remote-SSH comes on Friday"}
The **Remote — SSH** and **Remote Explorer** extensions are for connecting VS Code to the Talapas cluster — you will install and use them in [Module 09](Tutorial_09_SLURM_Basics.html) on Friday morning. No need to install them today.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Open a project folder

VS Code is folder-centric: almost everything works better when you open the root folder of a project rather than individual files.

1.  Download or clone the workshop repository so it is somewhere on your laptop (e.g. `~/scRNAseq_tutorial`).
2.  In VS Code choose **File → Open Folder…** (macOS: **File → Open…**) and navigate to that folder.
3.  The **Explorer** panel on the left now shows the folder tree. Click on any file to open it.
4.  VS Code may ask if you trust the authors of the files in this folder — click **Yes, I trust the authors** to enable full functionality.

::: {.callout-tip title="Workspace vs. folder"}
A **folder** opened directly is the simplest way to work. A **workspace** (`.code-workspace` file) lets you group multiple root folders — handy when a project spans several directories, but unnecessary for this workshop. Stick with **Open Folder** for now.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Edit a .qmd file and use the Quarto extension

1.  In the Explorer, open **Exercise_Folder → Tutorial_P1_Computer_Systems.qmd** (this file!).
2.  With the Quarto extension installed, VS Code shows a **Preview** button in the top-right corner of the editor tab. Click it — or press **Ctrl+Shift+K** / **Cmd+Shift+K** — to render a live HTML preview in a side panel.
3.  Edit a line of prose in the `.qmd` source and save (**Ctrl+S** / **Cmd+S**). The preview panel refreshes automatically.
4.  Find a code chunk (a block that starts with ` ```{r} ` or ` ```{bash} `). You can run it in-place with the **Run Cell** button (▶) that appears above the chunk, or by pressing **Ctrl+Enter** / **Cmd+Enter** with the cursor inside the chunk. The output appears below the chunk in the editor.

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
The YAML header at the top of this file sets `eval: false`. You ran a chunk anyway using the ▶ button. What is the difference between running a chunk interactively and rendering the whole document?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

**Running a chunk interactively** (▶ or Ctrl+Enter) executes it **right now in the active R session**, regardless of the chunk's `eval:` setting. `eval: false` only suppresses execution during a full **render** pass (when Quarto knits the whole document top-to-bottom into HTML/PDF). This is intentional in workshop tutorials: the published HTML shows the code without running it, but you can still step through it interactively. For your own analyses you will usually want `eval: true` so the rendered document reproduces all your results from scratch.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Use the integrated terminal locally

VS Code has a built-in terminal so you can run shell commands without switching windows.

1.  Open it with **Terminal → New Terminal** (or `` Ctrl+` ``). A terminal panel appears at the bottom, starting in the folder you opened.
2.  Run a few orientation commands:

```{bash}
#| label: P1-local_orientation
#| eval: false
pwd          # confirm you are in the workshop folder
ls           # list files
R --version  # confirm R is on your PATH
```

3.  If `R --version` returns "command not found", R is not on your system `PATH`. On macOS you may need to add `/usr/local/bin` or the path printed by `R RHOME`; on Windows, re-run the R installer and check "Add R to PATH" during setup.

::: {.callout-tip title="Terminal shortcut"}
Press `` Ctrl+` `` (backtick) to toggle the integrated terminal open and closed. This is one of the most useful VS Code shortcuts.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Run R locally from the integrated terminal

The integrated terminal is a full shell — you can start an interactive R session or run a script with `Rscript` exactly as you would on any Linux/macOS/Windows terminal.

**Start an interactive R session:**

```{bash}
#| label: P1-r_interactive
#| eval: false
R
```

Inside R, try a quick test:

```{r}
#| label: P1-r_hello
#| eval: false
cat("Hello from R on", Sys.info()[["nodename"]], "\n")
x <- rnorm(100)
summary(x)
q()          # quit R, return to the shell
```

**Run a script with Rscript:**

```{bash}
#| label: P1-rscript_local
#| eval: false
# From the Exercise_Folder, run the demo script locally
Rscript scripts/hello_world.R
```

You should see output like:

``` text
Hello from <your-laptop-name> at 2026-06-09 10:14:02
R version: R version 4.4.1 ...
Wrote hello_world_plot.pdf and hello_world_summary.csv
```

Two files are written in your current directory: `hello_world_plot.pdf` and `hello_world_summary.csv`. **Open them in VS Code:** double-click each in the Explorer panel. The PDF viewer extension renders the plot; the Excel Viewer shows the CSV as a table.

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
The output says `Hello from <your-laptop-name>`. On Friday, after you connect to Talapas and run the same script on a compute node, what will it say instead — and why does that matter?

<details><summary>Show answers</summary>

On Talapas it will say `Hello from n0123` (or whatever compute node SLURM allocated). The script prints `Sys.info()[["nodename"]]`, so the hostname tells you exactly **where the code ran** — your laptop, a login node, or a compute node. Confirming you are on a **compute node** (not a login node) is the proof that your SLURM job ran where it should. See [Module 09](Tutorial_09_SLURM_Basics.html) §7.5 for the cluster version of this test.

</details>
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Useful VS Code habits for the workshop

A few settings and shortcuts that will save you time across the week:

| What | How |
|---|---|
| Toggle word wrap | **View → Word Wrap** or **Alt+Z** |
| Find in current file | **Ctrl+F** / **Cmd+F** |
| Find across all files | **Ctrl+Shift+F** / **Cmd+Shift+F** |
| Go to a line number | **Ctrl+G** / **Cmd+G** |
| Format a file | **Shift+Alt+F** / **Shift+Option+F** |
| Open a new terminal | **Ctrl+Shift+`** / **Cmd+Shift+`** |
| Split editor pane | **Ctrl+\\** / **Cmd+\\** — useful to see a .qmd and its preview side-by-side |
| Open Command Palette | **Ctrl+Shift+P** / **Cmd+Shift+P** |

::: {.callout-tip title="Settings sync"}
If you use VS Code on multiple machines (laptop + lab desktop), turn on **Settings Sync** (**File → Preferences → Turn on Settings Sync…**) so your extensions and keybindings follow you automatically.
:::
